claims.text: As-synthesized HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure with multiscale phase features and inherent microstructural complexity.
A hybrid model can combine high-fidelity atomistic or mesoscopic simulation data with machine learning.
The model can incorporate quantitative descriptors such as nanoprecipitate size and distribution, phase-boundary density, and defect statistics.
The hybrid framework can be trained using both detailed simulation subsets and in situ tensile or fracture measurements.
Nanoprecipitates, phase boundaries, and defect-density distributions mediate dislocation motion.
Nanoprecipitates, phase boundaries, and defect-density distributions mediate crack initiation and propagation.
Explicit microstructural descriptors allow machine learning to capture complex multiscale interactions governing the mechanical response.
The hybrid approach reduces reliance on computationally expensive full-scale simulations.
The hybrid model will reduce computation time by approximately 50–70% relative to traditional multiscale simulations.
The model will predict Young's modulus of HfNbTiVAl10 within ±5% of experiment.
The model will predict yield strength of HfNbTiVAl10 within ±5% of experiment.
The model will accurately forecast fracture initiation and crack-propagation characteristics of HfNbTiVAl10.
Conventional atomistic or continuum simulations are computationally expensive.
Conventional simulations oversimplify the microstructural heterogeneity of HfNbTiVAl10 and consequently produce larger prediction errors.
Incomplete microstructural descriptors may cause the hybrid model to fail.
Adiabatic heating or unforeseen phase transformations under high strain rates or non-standard conditions may cause the model to fail.
A calibration dataset that is not representative of service conditions may cause the model to fail.
Related HEA and RCCA studies suggest that machine learning can predict yield-related and elastic properties.
